2Math Inquirers · Extension Workbook · About this book
Level 4Extension Workbook
Welcome!
This book is for you to explore at your own pace. Every unit has 7 pages. You can start on your own. A grown-up can help if you like.

How to use this book

  1. Read the Learn it page first. It shows how the idea works.
  2. Do the Start here pages. Use a pencil. Mistakes help you learn.
  3. Stuck? Find the hint. It is printed upside down.
  4. Do Check yourself. Check the answers. Wrong? Read the Why.

For the grown-up

  • Practice for the same ideas as the Holiday Program (our school-holiday course), with new numbers and stories. You do not need to have joined it: every unit starts with an example.
  • 3 short sessions a week, 25 to 30 minutes each, plus the weekend page Go further (see the pace plan).
  • This is a self-study book. Your child marks their own work: each answer at the back says the answer first, then a short reason (Why) in plain words, and the page of the question. A child who reads slowly may like a helper to read the Why with them. The answers start on page 79: please ask your child to try first.
  • Check yourself score 2 or less? Read the Learn it page again and redo one Start here page.
  • You will need: a pencil, a rubber, a ruler and a protractor.
  • Beyond Level 4 is ahead of school. You may skip it.
  • Print at 100 percent so the angles in Unit 6 are true size.

The four page names

Start here. The main path. Do these first.
Think harder. Longer problems. Hints are printed upside down.
Go further. A weekend page. Big challenges, just for fun.
Check yourself. Four quick questions at the end.

5Math Inquirers · Extension Workbook · Pace plan
Level 4Unit 1 · Factor HuntersName
Learn it: Factors and multiples
My goal. I can list every factor of a number in order. I can find common factors and common multiples and use them to solve sharing and timetable puzzles.
A factor goes into a number exactly. A multiple is in a times table. Write factors in pairs, in order, and stop when the pairs meet.
Worked example 1
Find all the factors of 54.
  1. Try 1, 2, 3 in order. Write a pair each time the number goes in.
  2. 4 and 5 do not go into 54. 6 × 9 = 54 is a pair.
  3. 7 and 8 do not go in, and the next number, 9, is already used. The pairs have met, so stop.
Answer: The factors of 54 are 1, 2, 3, 6, 9, 18, 27, 54.
Worked example 2
Lamp A flashes every 4 seconds. Lamp B flashes every 10 seconds. They flash together now. After how many seconds do they next flash together?
  1. List the multiples of each number.
  2. Find the first number in both lists.
Answer: They next flash together after 20 seconds.
How to hunt
  1. Factors: try 1, 2, 3 in order. Stop when the pairs meet.
  2. Common factors: list both numbers, then pick the numbers in both lists.
  3. Common multiples: list the multiples of both. The first number in both lists is the least.
Good to know
  • A pair like 6 × 6 counts as one factor.
  • So 36 has 9 factors, an odd number.
Your turnAnswer at the back of the book.
Try
Write all the factors of 45, in order.

12Math Inquirers · Extension Workbook · Unit 1 · Check yourself
Level 4Unit 2 · Big Number PuzzlesName
Learn it: Numbers to 100 000
My goal. I can round numbers to the nearest 10, 100 and 1000. I can work backwards from a rounded number and solve digit puzzles.
To round a number, find the two neighbours it lies between. Halfway rounds up. To work backwards from a rounded number, find the smallest and the largest numbers that round to it.
Worked example 1
Round 46 382 to the nearest 1000.
  1. 46 382 is between 46 000 and 47 000.
  2. The halfway mark is 46 500. 46 382 is before it.
Answer: 46 382 rounds to 46 000.
Worked example 2
A number rounds to 8000 to the nearest 1000. What are the smallest and the largest it can be?
  1. 7500 is halfway, so it rounds up to 8000.
  2. 8500 rounds up to 9000, so the last number is 8499.
Answer: Smallest 7500 and largest 8499.
How to round
  1. Find the 2 neighbours, such as 46 000 and 47 000.
  2. Find the halfway number. Halfway rounds up.
  3. To work backwards, find where the rounding changes.
Place value
  • 35 206 = 30 000 + 5000 + 200 + 6
  • Halfway rounds up: 46 500 goes up to 47 000.
Your turnAnswer at the back of the book.
Try
Round 52 718 to the nearest 100.

19Math Inquirers · Extension Workbook · Unit 2 · Check yourself
Level 4Unit 3 · Operation DetectivesName
Learn it: Four operations
My goal. I can solve multi-step problems with the four operations. I can use bar models for "times as many" and work backwards through a number machine.
A bar model shows a "times as many" story. Each equal part is one unit. To go back to the start of a number machine, undo each step in the opposite order.
Worked example 1
Mr Tan has 3 times as many red pens as blue pens. He has 156 pens in all. How many blue pens does he have?
  1. Blue is 1 unit and red is 3 units. That is 4 units.
  2. 4 units = 156, so 1 unit = 156 ÷ 4 = 39.
Answer: He has 39 blue pens.
Worked example 2
I think of a number. I add 9 and then multiply by 4. The answer is 68. What is my number?
  1. Undo the steps in the opposite order.
  2. Undo × 4 with ÷ 4: 68 ÷ 4 = 17. Undo + 9 with − 9: 17 − 9 = 8.
Answer: My number is 8. Check: 8 + 9 = 17 and 17 × 4 = 68.
How to solve it
  1. Bar models: draw one bar for each quantity. Count the units.
  2. Divide the total by the number of units.
  3. Machines: start from the end and undo each step. Check by going forward.
Opposites
  • + and − undo each other.
  • × and ÷ undo each other.
  • "4 times as many" is 4 units.
Your turnAnswer at the back of the book.
Try
A shop has 114 pens and rulers. The number of pens is 5 times the number of rulers. How many rulers are there?

26Math Inquirers · Extension Workbook · Unit 3 · Check yourself
Level 4Unit 4 · Fraction FrontierName
Learn it: Fractions
My goal. I can change between improper fractions and mixed numbers. I can find a fraction of a set and compare fractions with different denominators.
A fraction bar shows equal parts of one whole. A fraction of a set uses a bar model: divide the total by the denominator to find 1 unit.
Worked example 1
Write 17/5 as a mixed number.
  1. 5 fifths make 1 whole. Divide: 17 ÷ 5 = 3 with 2 left.
  2. There are 3 wholes and 2 fifths.
Answer: 17/5 = 3 2/5.
Worked example 2
There are 48 stickers. 5/6 of them are gold. How many are gold?
  1. 6 units = 48, so 1 unit = 48 ÷ 6 = 8.
  2. Gold is 5 units: 5 × 8 = 40.
Answer: 40 stickers are gold.
How to do it
  1. Improper to mixed: divide the top by the bottom.
  2. Mixed to improper: whole × bottom + top, over the bottom.
  3. Fraction of a set: 1 unit is the total ÷ the bottom number.
Comparing
  • Same bottom: the greater top is more.
  • Same top: the smaller bottom is more.
  • Or compare with 1/2.
  • Equivalent: multiply or divide top and bottom by the same number.
  • Whole from a part: 3 units = 36, so 1 unit = 12.
Your turnAnswer at the back of the book.
Try
Write 3 4/5 as an improper fraction. /

33Math Inquirers · Extension Workbook · Unit 4 · Check yourself
Level 4Unit 5 · Decimal DetectivesName
Learn it: Decimals
My goal. I can read decimals on number lines, compare and order them and round them. I can solve money and mass puzzles with bar models.
On a number line, first find what one small step is worth. To compare decimals, line up the decimal points and compare place by place from the left.
Worked example 1
What number does the arrow show?
  1. 4.5 to 4.6 has 10 steps. 1 step = 0.01.
  2. The arrow is 7 steps after 4.5.
Answer: The arrow shows 4.57.
Worked example 2
A number has 2 decimal places. It rounds to 6.3 to 1 decimal place. What are the least and greatest it can be?
  1. 6.25 is halfway, so it rounds up to 6.3.
  2. 6.35 rounds up to 6.4, so the last number is 6.34.
Answer: Least 6.25 and greatest 6.34.
How to do it
  1. Number line: find what 1 small step is worth.
  2. Compare: line up the points. Add zeros to fill the gaps.
  3. Round: find the 2 neighbours. Halfway rounds up.
Place value
  • 3.405 has 4 tenths, 0 hundredths and 5 thousandths.
Your turnAnswer at the back of the book.
Try

40Math Inquirers · Extension Workbook · Unit 5 · Check yourself
Level 4Unit 6 · Angle TurnsName
Learn it: Angles
My goal. I can measure angles and find missing angles. I can find the angle between clock hands and turn on the 8-point compass.
You need a 180° protractor and a ruler for this unit. A full turn is 360°, a half turn is 180° and a quarter turn is 90°. To measure, count up from the 0 on one arm.
Worked example 1
How big is the angle? Use the scale that starts at 0 on the arm.
  1. Put the centre of the protractor on the corner. Put the 0 line on one arm.
  2. Read the scale that starts at 0 on that arm.
Answer: The angle is 55°.
Worked example 2
What is the angle between the clock hands at 4 o'clock?
  1. A clock has 12 equal spaces in 360°. 360 ÷ 12 = 30, so 1 space is 30°.
  2. At 4 o'clock the hands are 4 spaces apart: 4 × 30°.
Answer: The angle is 120°.
How to measure
  1. Estimate first. Is it less than 90° or more?
  2. Centre on the corner. 0 line on one arm.
  3. Read from the 0 on that arm. Check with your estimate.
Good to know
  • Compass: 1 step = 45°.
  • Clock: 1 space = 30°.
  • Minute hand: 1 minute = 6°.
  • ∠AOC is the angle at O between OA and OC.
Your turnAnswer at the back of the book.
Try
Ali faces NE. He turns 135° clockwise. Which way does he face now? ESESSW

47Math Inquirers · Extension Workbook · Unit 6 · Check yourself
Level 4Unit 7 · Area Architects IIName
Learn it: Area and perimeter
My goal. I can find the area and the perimeter of shapes with square corners. I can compare rectangles with the same area.
Area is the space inside a shape, in cm². Perimeter is the distance round the edge, in cm. For a shape with square corners, take a piece away from a big rectangle, or split it into rectangles.
Worked example 1
The shape has square corners. Find its area and its perimeter.
  1. Big rectangle: 10 × 6 = 60. The missing corner is 4 × 2 = 8. Area = 60 − 8 = 52.
  2. Push the steps out to make a rectangle. The perimeter is 10 + 6 + 10 + 6 = 32.
Answer: Area 52 cm². Perimeter 32 cm.
Worked example 2
Rectangles with whole-cm sides have an area of 18 cm². Find the perimeter of each one.
  1. List the pairs that multiply to 18 in order: 1 × 18, 2 × 9, 3 × 6.
  2. Perimeter = 2 × (length + width).
Answer: The smallest perimeter is 18 cm, from 6 cm by 3 cm.
How to do it
  1. Missing sides: use the opposite sides.
  2. Area: split into rectangles, or take a piece away.
  3. Perimeter: push the steps out to a rectangle.
Good to know
  • Rectangle: area = length × width.
  • Perimeter = 2 × (length + width).
  • A square has 4 equal sides.
Your turnAnswer at the back of the book.
Try
A rectangle is 12 cm long and 5 cm wide. A 3 cm by 2 cm corner is cut off. What is the area of the shape that is left? cm²

54Math Inquirers · Extension Workbook · Unit 7 · Check yourself
Level 4Unit 8 · Symmetry and NetsName
Learn it: Symmetry and nets
My goal. I can tell which nets fold into a cube and which faces are opposite. I can complete a figure so that a line is a line of symmetry.
A net is a flat shape that folds into a solid. A cube net has 6 squares. In a line of 3 squares, the 2 end squares are opposite faces. On a dice, opposite faces add up to 7.
Worked example 1
Does this net fold into a cube? Which face is opposite P?
  1. Choose a base. The row of 4 squares wraps round as walls.
  2. One square is above the row and one is below. They make the lid and the base.
  3. P and R have 1 square between them. They are opposite.
Answer: It folds into a cube. R is opposite P.
Worked example 2
Complete the figure. The dashed line must be a line of symmetry.
  1. Flip each shaded square across the line.
  2. The partner is the same distance from the line.
Answer: Each shaded square gets a partner the same distance from the line.
How to do it
  1. Net: choose a base. Fold the squares round it in your head.
  2. A net needs 1 base, 1 lid and 4 walls.
  3. Symmetry: count squares from the line to the partner.
Good to know
  • Dice: opposite faces add up to 7.
  • A rectangle has 2 lines of symmetry. A square has 4.
  • No fold: 4 squares at one corner, or 5 in a row.
Your turnAnswer at the back of the book.
Try
Opposite faces of a dice add up to 7. What number is opposite 4?

61Math Inquirers · Extension Workbook · Unit 8 · Check yourself
Level 4Unit 9 · Data DetectivesName
Learn it: Tables and line graphs
My goal. I can read values and changes on line graphs. I can find missing numbers in tables and spot graphs with scales that mislead.
On a line graph, read the title and the scale first. The change between 2 neighbouring points is the difference of their values. A table can have a missing number: use the totals to find it.
Worked example 1
The graph shows the cups of barley water a stall sold. Each line is worth 10. How many cups were sold on Wednesday? When was the greatest drop?
  1. The Wednesday point is halfway between 50 and 60: 55 cups.
  2. Find each change. Thu to Fri is 75 − 30 = 45 down. That is the greatest drop.
Answer: 55 cups. The greatest drop was Thursday to Friday.
Worked example 2
Find the missing number. Each row and each column adds to its total.
  1. Use Ali's row: 14 + ? = 31, so ? = 31 − 14 = 17.
  2. Check the Week 2 column: 17 + 18 = 35.
Answer: The missing number is 17.
How to read data
  1. Read the title and the scale. What is one line worth?
  2. Change = the difference between 2 neighbours.
  3. Missing numbers: use the row or column total.
Good to know
  • The steepest line is the greatest change.
  • Check where each scale starts.
Your turnAnswer at the back of the book.

68Math Inquirers · Extension Workbook · Unit 9 · Check yourself
Level 4Unit 10 · Puzzle DayName
Learn it: Mixed puzzle heuristics
My goal. I can choose a way in to a puzzle: guess and check, suppose all are the same, work backwards, draw it or use a logic grid.
A puzzle needs a way in. Guess and check with a table: use each try to decide whether to go up or down. Suppose all are the same: then see how many swaps you need to fix the total.
Worked example 1
A shop has stools (3 legs) and chairs (4 legs). There are 11 of them with 38 legs in all. How many chairs are there?
  1. Each swap from a stool to a chair adds 1 leg.
  2. 5 legs short needs 5 swaps.
Answer: 5 chairs and 6 stools. Check: 5 × 4 + 6 × 3 = 38.
Worked example 2
Two next-door numbers multiply to 380. What are they?
  1. Try a pair. Is the product too big or too small?
  2. Use each try to choose the next one.
Answer: The numbers are 19 and 20.
Ways in
  1. Guess and check: keep a table of tries.
  2. Suppose all are the same. Count swaps.
  3. Work backwards: undo the last step first.
  4. Check your answer against every fact.
Good to know
  • Draw a queue or a bar model.
  • Check the answer against every clue.
  • A swap changes the total by a fixed amount.
  • Logic grid: ✓ for yes, ✗ for no. One ✓ in each row and column.
Your turnAnswer at the back of the book.
Try
